title: Central Limit Theorem with Finite Population Correction
scenario_markdown: An internal audit team at a regional commercial bank reviews a branch portfolio consisting of exactly $N = 400$ commercial loan accounts. Across these 400 accounts, loan balances have population mean $\mu = \$50,000$ and standard deviation $\sigma = \$8,000$. The auditor draws a simple random sample of $n = 64$ loan files without replacement.
assumptions: Simple random sampling without replacement from a finite population of size N = 400
Sample size n = 64 satisfies n / N = 64 / 400 = 0.16 > 0.05, requiring the Finite Population Correction (FPC)
Sample size n = 64 >= 30, so the sample mean X_bar is approximately normally distributed by the Central Limit Theorem
source_refs: Course Module 4: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

approval.notes: Verified FPC calculation: N = 400, n = 64. Fraction n/N = 0.16 > 0.05 requires FPC. FPC factor = sqrt(336 / 399) = 0.917663. Uncorrected SE = 8000 / 8 = 1000. Corrected SE = 1000 * 0.917663 = 917.66.

stages.prompt_markdown: Why must the auditor apply the Finite Population Correction (FPC) factor when calculating the standard error of the sample mean?

options.text_markdown: Sampling is conducted without replacement and the sampling fraction $\frac{n}{N} = \frac{64}{400} = 0.16$ ($16\%$) exceeds the $5\%$ ($0.05$) threshold.
FPC is applied whenever sample size is less than 100, regardless of population size $N$.
options.hint_markdown: FPC depends strictly on the sampling fraction $n/N$; if $N = 1{,}000{,}000$, a sample of $n = 64$ would not require FPC because $n/N < 0.05$.

options.text_markdown: FPC is required whenever sampling is conducted with replacement.
options.hint_markdown: Sampling with replacement preserves population probabilities, treating the population as effectively infinite (FPC = 1.0). FPC is only used when sampling WITHOUT replacement.

stages.explanation_markdown: When sampling without replacement from a finite population of size $N$, observations are not strictly independent. Standard practice dictates that whenever the sample represents more than $5\%$ of the population ($n/N > 0.05$), the finite population correction factor $\sqrt{\frac{N - n}{N - 1}}$ must be applied. Here $\frac{64}{400} = 0.16 = 16\% > 5\%$, so FPC is necessary.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the value of the Finite Population Correction (FPC) multiplier for this audit sample?

options.hint_markdown: $0.8421$ is the variance correction factor $(N-n)/(N-1)$. Standard error requires taking the square root: $\sqrt{0.8421} \approx 0.9177$.
The correct formula is $\sqrt{\frac{N - n}{N - 1}}$, not a linear subtraction $1 - n/N$.

stages.explanation_markdown: The FPC factor is $\sqrt{\frac{N - n}{N - 1}} = \sqrt{\frac{400 - 64}{399}} = \sqrt{\frac{336}{399}} \approx \sqrt{0.842105} \approx 0.9177$. This multiplier adjusts the standard error downward to account for the finite population.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the corrected standard error of the sample mean $\sigma_{\bar{x}}$, and why is it smaller than the uncorrected standard error?

options.text_markdown: $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \times \text{FPC} = \frac{8{,}000}{8} \times 0.9177 = \$917.66$; it is smaller because sampling without replacement depletes the remaining unobserved accounts, reducing sampling uncertainty.
$\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{8{,}000}{\sqrt{64}} = \$1{,}000.00$; FPC only affects confidence intervals, not standard error.
options.hint_markdown: $\$1{,}000.00$ is the uncorrected standard error for an infinite population. FPC directly multiplies the standard error, reducing it to $\$917.66$.
The denominator of the standard error is $\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{64} = 8$, not $\sqrt{N}$.

stages.explanation_markdown: The uncorrected standard error is $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{8{,}000}{\sqrt{64}} = \$1{,}000.00$. Multiplying by the FPC factor gives the corrected standard error $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 1{,}000 \times 0.917663 = \$917.66$. Sampling without replacement reduces uncertainty because each sampled account provides exact information and removes variability from the remaining unobserved population.
